newsitem.title: FRANCE: Boeing deal avoids war, puts onus on Airbus.
newsitem.headline: Boeing deal avoids war, puts onus on Airbus.

text.p: A European Union decision to allow a $15 billion merger between Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas has avoided a transatlantic trade war and stressed the need for a decision on the future of Airbus, officials said on Wednesday.

German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said he was happy a trade war had been averted. "I am happy that the theatened trade conflict between Europe and the U.S. could be avoided through last-minute concessions by Boeing," he said in a statement.
Boeing dropped exclusive supply contracts with AMR Corp's American Airlines, Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines.
Rexrodt said Boeing, despite the concessions, would dominate the world aerospace industry which made it necessary for Europe's four-nation Airbus consortium to restructure.
"The first step must be a reorganisation of (Europe's) Airbus Industrie from a loose consortium to a unified corporation, at best in the form of a public company," he added.

French Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine said the European Union's firmness in the Boeing/McDonnell Douglas negotiations had paid off. "Nobody was looking for a trade war, in any case not the European Union," he told RTL radio.

"It is in the name of international rules of competition in the European market, which have to be respected by all players including American companies, that the (European) Commission has examined this merger," Vedrine said.
"It seems that this firmness has led Boeing to make extremely important concessions."
Airbus Industrie postponed formal comment until a final decision by the European Commission next week, but said in a critical first reaction that it regretted U.S. "arrogance".

"Airbus Industrie regrets ... the arrogant and confrontational attitude of the U.S.A. in these discussions," Airbus spokesman Alain Dupeich told Reuters by telephone from Toulouse in southwestern France.
Financial analysts had mixed opinions on whether the Boeing concessions were important or just a bargaining chip.

"The fact is that in the civil aircraft industry you buy an airliner for 25 years. You have massive investment and you get massive economies from single types," Chris Avery, aerospace analyst at Paribas in London, told Reuters Financial Television.
"The economic effect of these deals will continue even if the terms get dropped from the contracts," he added.
In fact, Continental Airlines Inc said it did not intend to alter its plans to buy aircraft exclusively from Boeing, which is based in Seattle, Washington.
An analyst at a Paris-based brokerage said on the contrary that the removal of the exclusivity clause was important.

"The exclusive contracts were the big worry to me," he said. "With the exclusive supply contracts Airbus would have virtually been kept off the U.S. market. Now they stand to win orders there, as they have shown in the past they can."
"The aerospace industry in Europe has seen no consolidation at all by comparison with the massive moves that have taken place in the U.S.A. in the last four years," Paribas' Avery said.
"The single most important thing that would help Airbus to gain market share against Boeing is to reform itself and become more competitive.

The French analyst said airlines would prefer to keep a balance between the two suppliers and the balance of power would "almost mechanically" switch from the current 65/35 percent to 55/45 percent in favour of Boeing.
In 1996, Boeing obtained 66 percent of new aircraft orders, McDonnell four percent and Airbus 30 percent.

Toulouse-based Airbus Industrie is a consortium made up of French state-owned Societe Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain.
The four companies and the governments of the member countries have agreed that Airbus should become a proper company with its own balance sheet and results.
However the participating companies still disagree about which assets to transfer to Airbus, and at what price.
